steps.title: Import console and performance APIs
steps.instruction: In JavaScript, you can directly use browser APIs like console and performance without import statements. Write a simple function named measurePerformance that logs a message to the console using console.log and accesses the performance.now() method.
steps.hint: Create a function that logs a message and calls performance.now(). No imports are needed in plain JavaScript.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named measurePerformance is created that uses console.log and performance.now() to log performance data.
successCriteria: The function measurePerformance is defined, uses console.log, and calls performance.now() without any import statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a function that uses browser APIs directly. This demonstrates that console and performance are globally available in JavaScript environments.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named measurePerformance and includes both console.log and performance.now().
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your function name and syntax. Remember, you don't need import statements for console and performance in plain JavaScript.

steps.title: Create main function to demonstrate memory concepts
steps.instruction: Create a function named 'main' that will serve as the main execution context for our performance and memory examples. The function should be empty for now.
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or an arrow function. Just make sure it's named 'main' and has an empty body.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: a named function with empty body
function setup() {}
steps.seedCode:
// Write your measurePerformance function here

// Create your main function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named 'main' is created and ready to contain our performance examples.
successCriteria: A function named 'main' exists in the code with an empty body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the main function that will hold our performance and memory examples.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a function named 'main' with an empty body.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main function wasn't created correctly. Please create a function named 'main' with an empty body.

steps.title: Initialize variables to demonstrate memory allocation
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create four variables: a string, a number, an array, and an object.
steps.hint: Declare variables using const or let, assigning each a value of the appropriate type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will contain four variables representing different JavaScript data types.
successCriteria: The main function contains a string variable, a number variable, an array variable, and an object variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created variables that will allocate memory for different data types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some variables, but make sure you have all four types: string, number, array, and object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've declared four variables with the correct data types inside the main function.

steps.title: Create memory leak example with detached DOM references
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, create a function named createDetachedReferences that creates a DOM element and stores it in a global variable to simulate a memory leak.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates a div element using document.createElement and assigns it to a variable declared outside the function scope.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that demonstrates how keeping references to DOM elements outside their intended scope can cause memory leaks.
successCriteria: The createDetachedReferences function exists inside main, creates a DOM element, and assigns it to a variable that persists beyond the function's scope.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a function that simulates a memory leak by keeping a reference to a DOM element. This demonstrates how detached references prevent garbage collection.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function creates a DOM element and stores it in a way that prevents garbage collection (like assigning to a global variable).
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't properly demonstrate a memory leak. It should create a DOM element and keep a reference to it that persists beyond the function's execution.

steps.title: Create performance measurement function
steps.instruction: Create a function named measurePerformance that takes a callback function as a parameter and uses performance.now() to measure how long it takes to execute that callback.
steps.hint: Inside the function, record a start time, execute the callback, record an end time, then calculate and return the difference.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a measurePerformance function that can be used to time any callback function's execution.
successCriteria: The measurePerformance function is defined, takes a callback parameter, uses performance.now() to measure execution time, and returns the duration.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a performance measurement function that uses the Performance API.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes a callback parameter, calls performance.now() before and after executing it, and returns the time difference.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Review the example: you need to capture start/end times with performance.now() and calculate the difference after executing the callback.

steps.title: Create synchronous blocking function
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a function named simulateBlocking that performs a heavy synchronous computation (like a large loop) to demonstrate blocking behavior.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses a for loop to iterate many times, performing a simple operation inside the loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named simulateBlocking is defined inside main, ready to demonstrate synchronous blocking behavior.
successCriteria: The simulateBlocking function is defined with a loop that performs many iterations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a synchronous blocking function. This will help demonstrate how heavy synchronous code can block the event loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but it might not perform enough computation to clearly demonstrate blocking. Ensure it has a loop with many iterations.
steps.feedbackWrong: The simulateBlocking function is not defined correctly. Make sure to create a function inside main that performs heavy synchronous computation.

steps.title: Create asynchronous non-blocking function
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, create a new function named simulateNonBlocking that uses setTimeout to demonstrate non-blocking asynchronous behavior.
steps.hint: Use setTimeout to schedule a callback that logs a message after a delay, showing how async code allows other operations to continue.
steps.expectedOutcome: A simulateNonBlocking function is added to main that uses setTimeout to demonstrate non-blocking behavior.
successCriteria: The simulateNonBlocking function is defined inside main and uses setTimeout with a callback.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created an asynchronous function that demonstrates how setTimeout allows the event loop to continue processing other tasks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function uses setTimeout and is properly defined inside the main function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Remember to define simulateNonBlocking inside main and use setTimeout with a callback function.

steps.title: Create microtask example with Promise
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a new function called demonstrateMicrotask that uses a Promise to show microtask queue behavior.
steps.hint: Define a function that returns a Promise and logs messages to demonstrate microtask execution order.
steps.expectedOutcome: A demonstrateMicrotask function is added to main that returns a Promise and logs messages about microtasks.
successCriteria: The demonstrateMicrotask function is defined inside main and returns a Promise.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a function that demonstrates microtask behavior using Promises.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure demonstrateMicrotask returns a Promise and is defined inside main.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function demonstrateMicrotask should be created inside main and return a Promise to show microtask behavior.

steps.title: Add console logging to track execution order
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, add console.log statements at the beginning of each function call to show when they execute relative to the event loop.
steps.hint: Add console.log('...') before each function call inside main() to log execution order.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will include console.log statements that visually demonstrate the execution order of synchronous, asynchronous, and microtask functions when run.
successCriteria: console.log statements are added inside main() before each function call to log execution order.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added console logging to track execution order. This will help visualize how synchronous, asynchronous, and microtask functions execute in the event loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some console.log statements, but make sure to add them before each function call inside main() to properly track execution order.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console.log statements aren't properly placed inside main() to track execution order. Add console.log('...') before each function call to show when they execute.

steps.title: Create function to demonstrate garbage collection
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a function named demonstrateGarbageCollection that allocates a large array and then releases the reference to it.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates a large data structure (like an array with many elements) and then sets the variable to null or lets it go out of scope.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that shows how memory can be allocated and then made eligible for garbage collection by removing references.
successCriteria: The demonstrateGarbageCollection function is defined inside main, creates a large array, and releases the reference (e.g., by setting to null or letting it go out of scope).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a function that demonstrates garbage collection by allocating memory and then releasing the reference.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined the function, but make sure it creates a large data structure and explicitly releases the reference (e.g., sets it to null).
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't demonstrate garbage collection properly. Ensure it allocates memory and then releases the reference.

steps.title: Wire up function calls in main execution
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, call all the previously created functions in this specific order to demonstrate event loop behavior: first call createDetachedReferences, then simulateBlocking, then simulateNonBlocking, then demonstrateMicrotask, then demonstrateGarbageCollection, and finally measurePerformance.
steps.hint: Add the function calls directly inside the main function body, one after another, in the order specified.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will execute all the performance, memory, and event loop examples in a specific sequence, showing how synchronous, asynchronous, and microtask code interact.
successCriteria: All six functions (createDetachedReferences, simulateBlocking, simulateNonBlocking, demonstrateMicrotask, demonstrateGarbageCollection, and measurePerformance) are called inside main() in the correct order.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've wired up all the function calls correctly. This demonstrates how different types of code execution interact in the event loop.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some function calls, but not all six in the correct order. Make sure to call createDetachedReferences, simulateBlocking, simulateNonBlocking, demonstrateMicrotask, demonstrateGarbageCollection, and measurePerformance in that exact sequence.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main function doesn't contain the required function calls in the correct order. Review the instruction and add calls to all six functions in the specified sequence.

steps.title: Execute the main function and observe console output
steps.instruction: Call the main function at the end of your script to execute all the performance, memory, and event loop demonstrations.
steps.hint: Simply write the function call after your main function definition.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will execute, showing console output that demonstrates memory allocation, performance timing, blocking vs non-blocking operations, microtask execution order, and garbage collection concepts.
successCriteria: The main function is called at the end of the script, triggering execution of all the demonstration functions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Calling main() executes all your performance, memory, and event loop demonstrations. Check the console to see the complete picture of execution order, timing measurements, and memory behavior.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're calling the main function with parentheses: main(). This executes the function you defined earlier.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to call the main function you created. Add main(); at the end of your script to execute all the demonstration functions.
